title: When the Well Breaks
premise: Orsen Quintana returns to the village of Hollowmere to bury their twin sister Wren, only to find that no one remembers Wren existed — and that the church bell, melted down in 1911, has begun ringing at dusk. The bell's song is a lure older than the village, sung by a congregation that was drowned beneath the millpond, and everyone who hears it starts humming along. Orsen discovers the song has a final verse that was never written down: whoever learns it without singing it can command the bell instead of obeying it. But the verse can only be learned by trading away a belonging — and Orsen must choose between the loyalty that ties them to their sister's ghost and the truth that Wren was the one who rang the bell first. In the end, Orsen sings the last verse alone, silences the bell, and lets Wren's ghost finally sink — keeping the village's lights on, but never again its doors.
about_author: Theo Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former church archivist who spent a decade cataloguing defunct parish records in rural England before turning to horror. Their work is known for liturgical dread and stories about communities that keep their promises long after they should have stopped.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sibling
chapters.summary: Orsen Quintana arrives in Hollowmere by bus, carrying their twin Wren's ashes, and finds the grave already dug with Wren's name on it. The vicar greets Orsen warmly but calls them 'the survivor' as if the funeral happened years ago. POV: Orsen. Beat: quiet wrongness, the sense of arriving late to one's own story.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Orsen moves into the family cottage and falls back into childhood rituals: counting doors, checking locks, keeping the lights on. Neighbors leave bread on the step but never knock. A child asks why Orsen hums at night — Orsen isn't humming. POV: Orsen. Beat: isolation sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: No Bell Since 1911
chapters.summary: At the parish archive, Orsen confirms the church bell was melted down for scrap in 1911; the tower has been empty for a century. The archivist, Mrs. Halloway, goes pale when Orsen mentions the ringing. She burns a page from the register in front of them. POV: Orsen. Beat: first hard evidence that the village knows and lies.

chapters.title: Dusk, and the Sound
chapters.summary: Orsen hears the bell at dusk for the first time — a deep, wet-toned peal with no source. The whole village stops mid-motion, faces tilting toward the pond. Orsen's teeth ache with the urge to hum along. They bite their tongue until it bleeds. POV: Orsen. Beat: dread made physical; the lure introduced.

chapters.title: The Congregation Below
chapters.summary: Orsen sees figures standing in the millpond at night, dressed in 1911 clothing, mouths open in perfect unison. Among them, a figure with Wren's posture. Orsen runs home and counts the doors twice; there are thirteen now. POV: Orsen. Beat: the horror acquires a face — and a family resemblance.

chapters.title: What the Bread Is For
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway confesses: the drowned congregation rings for new singers, and the bread on doorsteps is an old bargain — fed, they stay outside. But Orsen never ate the bread. She warns: the bell always gets its verse back. POV: alternating Orsen and Mrs. Halloway's diary. Beat: exposition as confession; the rules of the world established.

chapters.title: Wren, Humming
chapters.summary: Wren's ghost appears in the cottage, translucent and humming, unable to speak. She leads Orsen to a hidden score in the floorboards — the bell's song, four verses written, the fifth torn out. Wren points at the torn edge, then at Orsen's throat. POV: Orsen. Beat: grief and suspicion entwined; the quest object revealed.

chapters.title: The Verse That Wasn't Written
chapters.summary: Orsen researches the 1911 drowning: the congregation sang the millpond church under as it flooded, and the last verse was deliberately destroyed by the sexton so no one could ever command the bell again. The sexton's descendants still live in Hollowmere — the Halloways. POV: Orsen. Beat: the village's guilt surfaces; loyalty vs. truth begins to split.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Sing in Their Sleep
chapters.summary: Villagers begin sleepwalking to the pond, humming in harmony. The vicar nails his own shutters closed. A child goes missing and returns soaked, singing a verse Orsen has never heard — verse four-and-a-half, a fragment. The bell rings at noon now, not just dusk. POV: Orsen and the missing child, Tam. Beat: the contagion spreads; the clock starts ticking.

chapters.title: Halloway's Bargain
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway reveals her family's burden: each generation, one Halloway must stand at the pond and refuse the song aloud, holding the bell at bay. She is dying, and there is no successor. She offers to teach Orsen the refusals — but refuses, always, to speak of the fifth verse. POV: Mrs. Halloway, with Orsen present. Beat: an ally with a locked room in her heart.

chapters.title: The Pond Gives Back
chapters.summary: The pond begins returning things: a 1911 hymnal, a child's shoe, and a photograph of the drowned congregation — in which Wren stands, alive, dated last spring. Orsen realizes Wren came to Hollowmere before her death, and rang something. POV: Orsen. Beat: the twist turns grief into betrayal; loyalty cracks.

chapters.title: What Wren Did
chapters.summary: Through the ghost's gestures and the sexton's buried journal, Orsen reconstructs the truth: Wren, researching their family's tie to Hollowmere, found the torn verse, sang four verses at the pond, and the congregation took her voice — then her life. The bell has been ringing for her ever since. POV: Orsen. Beat: devastating midpoint revelation; the wrong sibling was buried twice.

chapters.title: Thirteen Doors
chapters.summary: The cottage's doors now number thirteen, and one of them is Wren's old bedroom door standing where no wall is. Behind it, humming. Orsen nails it shut; by morning the nails are on the pillow, arranged in a musical staff. POV: Orsen. Beat: the haunting turns intimate and architectural; no safe ground remains.

chapters.title: Tam's Verse
chapters.summary: Orsen coaxes the fragment out of Tam: it is the true beginning of the fifth verse, which can't be written or read — only passed mouth to mouth, and only to someone the congregation has marked. Tam's parents beg Orsen to unmark him. Orsen realizes the mark has transferred to them. POV: Tam, then Orsen. Beat: the cost of knowledge becomes a debt on the innocent.

chapters.title: The Refusal Lessons
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway teaches Orsen the Halloway refusals — counter-rhythms, cold iron on the tongue, the naming of the drowned one by one. Orsen is clumsy, nearly hums, and is saved only by biting down on the iron. Mrs. Halloway coughs blood and says the pond is hurrying because it knows she's almost done. POV: Orsen. Beat: training montage as ritual; competence earned at a price.

chapters.title: The Night of the Open Doors
chapters.summary: Every door in Hollowmere opens at once at dusk. The village walks to the pond in their nightclothes, singing. Orsen uses the refusals to hold the crowd at the waterline, but Mrs. Halloway, keeping her post, is pulled under — and the bell tolls a name: Quintana. POV: Orsen. Beat: midpoint battle lost; the ally sacrificed; Orsen is now the marked one.

chapters.title: Sinking Lessons
chapters.summary: Wren's ghost, more solid now, drags Orsen into the pond's edge — not to drown them but to show them: the congregation isn't malicious, only unfinished, singing a song that was cut off mid-word a century ago. The last verse isn't a command; it's an ending. To learn it, Orsen must give up a belonging. POV: Wren, in fragments. Beat: the monster reframed; grief becomes comprehension.

chapters.title: The Price of Belonging
chapters.summary: Orsen understands the trade: the bell takes what roots you. They catalog their belongings — the cottage, the counted doors, the rituals, Wren's ashes — and realize the congregation wants the deepest one: Orsen's belonging to Wren, the twin-bond itself. Wren, present, nods. POV: Orsen. Beat: the thematic choice made explicit; the sacrifice named.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: Over three nights, Wren teaches Orsen the fifth verse word by word, each word costing a memory of their childhood together. Orsen holds the melody in their mouth without ever letting it become song — the discipline of a lifetime of counted doors. The bell rings continuously now. POV: Orsen. Beat: climax approached through loss; every line learned is a line of love erased.

chapters.title: The Singing
chapters.summary: At the flooded hour, the whole village stands at the pond and the congregation rises. Orsen walks into the water up to the waist and sings the fifth verse alone — complete, unaccompanied, unsung-by. The bell cracks mid-peal. The congregation, finished at last, bows and goes down like lights going out. Wren, whole and voiceless still, touches Orsen's cheek and sinks with them. POV: Orsen. Beat: climax; power used not to rule the bell but to release it.

chapters.title: After the Silence
chapters.summary: The pond is still. The bell tower is empty again, and this time it stays empty. Orsen remembers Wren only as a fact, not a feeling — and finds that grief, even amputated, still aches in the shape of her. The villagers wake with no memory of the night, but they stop leaving bread. POV: Orsen. Beat: denouement; the cost tallied in absence.

chapters.title: Keeping the Lights On
chapters.summary: Orsen stays in Hollowmere, the new keeper of the refusals, teaching Tam the counter-rhythms. The doors in the cottage number twelve again, and Orsen counts them each night not from fear now, but as a prayer. On the last page, at dusk, Orsen listens — and hears nothing, and weeps without knowing why. POV: Orsen. Beat: resolution; belonging rebuilt on truth, loyalty transmuted into vigilance.
